results.note: UNESCO ICH page fetched; title phrase verbatim; inscribed 2016 (11.COM) Representative List.
Page: 'Gada is organized into five classes ... leadership changing on a rotational basis every eight years'. Evidence verbatim; own words.
Page: 'Knowledge about the Gada system is transmitted to children in the home and at school.' Evidence verbatim.
WHC page blocks WebFetch (403) but was read in the browser; Criterion (iii): terraces 'still actively used by the Konso people, who created them'; inscribed 2011.
Page: 'The cultural spaces inside the walled towns, called moras, retain an important and central role in the life of the Konso.' Evidence verbatim.
Page: 'The Konso erect stone steles to commemorate and mark the transfer of responsibility from the older generation to the younger' and 'living tradition of stele erection'.
Cultural Survival article (16 Jul 2025): 'The Anywaa are river cultivators and fishers' and 'rhythms of the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro), and Gilo Rivers'; Gambella named throughout.
Page: EMIPRO 'Founded in 2022 by Indigenous activists ... including Yousif Gilo (Anywaa)' and 'the first legally registered Indigenous-led organization in Ethiopia'. Evidence verbatim.

IWGIA 2024 Eritrea chapter: 'Afar State in Ethiopia, which has an Afar population of 1.8 million.22'; endnote 22 reads 'Ethiopia, Central Statistical Agency. This is a projection for 2017.' Government projection and as_of 2017 both confirmed.
IWGIA Eritrea chapter: 'at least four indigenous peoples: the Afar ..., Kunama, Saho and Nara. These groups have inhabited their traditional territories for approximately 2,000 years.'
pastoralists.org (12 Oct 2008): council 'set up in September 2008' as 'a means for Afar pastoralists to raise their voices both on a regional, national and international stage'. Evidence verbatim.

IWGIA Uganda chapter: 'The Mosopisyek Benet people, also referred to as Ndorobo, have inhabited Mount Elgon for over 500 years.' The chapter places the Benet in the 'north-eastern part of Uganda', not 'eastern'; region qualifier removed so the text matches the page.
results.text: The Mosopisyek Benet have lived on Mount Elgon in Uganda for more than five hundred years.
results.evidence: inhabited Mount Elgon for over 500 years

results.note: Cultural Survival (28 Dec 2005): Benet 'recognized as the historical, indigenous inhabitants of Mount Elgon ... by the country's High Court'; ruling dated 27 October (2005). Evidence verbatim.
IWGIA Uganda chapter: 'On 24 May 2023, the Office of the Prime Minister issued a directive ordering the UWA to cease evictions and raids on the community.' Evidence verbatim.

IWGIA Uganda chapter: 'Karamojong people - whose economy is traditionally based on livestock - live in the north-east of the country (mainly drylands) and have an estimated population of 1,094,100 according to a mid-2018 estimate by the Uganda Bureau of Statistics.' 1.09 million is a fair rounding.

Kara-Tunga page (11 Aug 2017): 'Cultural Heritage Clubs at 5 Secondary Schools located in the two central districts of Karamoja (Napak and Moroto)' and culture 'central to the history and identity of Karimojong'. Caveat: publisher is a tour operator partnering with CCFU; a CCFU page would be a stronger source.

Cultural Survival (2 Jun 2026), byline 'By Hai//om Community San Council and Roseline Genade Geises': 'many Hai//om communities lived in areas that are now part of Etosha National Park and surrounding regions.'
Page: 'rich cultural heritage that includes language, storytelling, music, traditional knowledge' and 'Mother-tongue-based education in early grades would improve comprehension and confidence.'

The Namibian (5 Aug 2026) publishes the VP speech dated 'Outjo, Kunene Region. 30 July 2026' at the 'High-Level Stakeholder Meeting on the Future of the Hai-//om San Community', addressing 'the Hai-//om Traditional Authority', calling for 'a comprehensive Livelihoods Options and Development Plan'. Newspaper record of a government speech; acceptable but lower tier than an official release.
IWGIA Zimbabwe chapter: Tshwa 'self-identify' as Indigenous, 'found in western Zimbabwe'; 'Population estimates indicate that there are 3,207 Tshwa and 1,579 Doma in Zimbabwe ... in 2023'.

IWGIA Zimbabwe chapter: '"Koisan" language is included in Zimbabwe's 2013 revised constitution as one of the 16 languages recognized' and 'Work was done on the Tjwao language by the Tsoro-o-tso San Development Trust in 2023.'
SAHO (du Plessis introduction): language 'referred to by its speakers as !Ora'; 'the Korana people would refer to themselves as either !Orakua ... or !Orana'. Evidence verbatim.
IWGIA South Africa chapter: 'the Koranna mainly in Kimberley and the Free State province'. Evidence verbatim.

SAHO: people in Bloemfontein 'were either directly or indirectly involved in the revival movement' and 'the idea of revitalising the Kora language was raised on more than one occasion'. Evidence verbatim.
IWGIA South Africa chapter: 'the Griqua in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal provinces'. Evidence verbatim.
SAHO Griqua article: 'a basic system of government based on leaders known as kaptyns and magistrates drawn from the leading families.' Evidence verbatim; own words.

Page: 'The Griquas founded a settlement called Klaarwater, later known as Griquatown.' Content supported, but the researcher's text was a near copy of the source sentence; rephrased into own words. Evidence unchanged.
results.text: Klaarwater, the settlement Griqua people founded, later took the name Griquatown.
results.evidence: The Griquas founded a settlement called Klaarwater, later known as Griquatown

results.note: IWGIA Cameroon chapter: 'The Bakola and Bagyeli live in an area of around 12,000 km2 in the south of Cameroon, particularly in the districts of Akom II, Bipindi, Kribi and Lolodorf.'

Forest Peoples Programme (7 Apr 2020): 'the Bagyeli have mapped their activities in the forest' and 'In November and December 2018, they submitted three Community Forest dossiers to the Divisional Delegation of the Ministry of Forests and Fauna (MINFOF).'

Cultural Survival Quarterly page: 'The Wodaabe's main economic activity is cattle-herding.' 'The seasons dictate Wodaabe migrations.' 'migrating through much of the Sahel'. Older article (CSQ archive); still accurate as a general statement.

MSH Mondes page for Sandrine Loncke's book: 'Au coeur du Sahel nigerien ... des milliers de Peuls nomades wodaabe se reunissent chaque annee pour un vaste rassemblement ceremoniel, dont le rituel central est appele geerewol' and 'les seules armes sont le chant et la danse'. Evidence verbatim (French).

pastoralists.org (12 Nov 2008): 'The fourth General Assembly of the Woodaabe Pastoralists of Niger took place this year from the 5th - 14th October. It was attended by thousands of Woodaabe pastoralists'.
OpenEdition (CNRS Editions, An Atlas of Contemporary Egypt, 2023): 'Ten tribes speaking an eastern Berber language (Siwi) inhabit the oases of Siwa and El-Gara.' Evidence verbatim.
Page: 'It is the furthest eastern outpost of the Tamazgha, the lands traditionally inhabited by the Berbers.' Evidence verbatim.

Page says 'A sense of Berber allegiance with its own particularities has been revived in the 21st century' then 'A letter from the Tifinagh alphabet, symbol of the Amazigh people, now marks the name of one of the bazaars at the foot of ancient Shali.' The phrase 'Amazigh identity has grown stronger' is not what the page says (it says revived); text tightened to the page. Evidence unchanged.
results.text: A sense of Berber belonging has revived in Siwa this century; a letter of the Tifinagh alphabet, the Amazigh symbol, now names a bazaar below old Shali.
results.evidence: A letter from the Tifinagh alphabet, symbol of the Amazigh people

results.note: HCP RGPH 2024 Tanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima PDF (text extracted locally after download): 'Le Tarifit est plus utilise a la province d'Al Hoceima (53,6%)'. Evidence verbatim across a line break. The page does not itself use the name Irifiyen; that linkage is the researcher's.

Table 'Langues locales utilisees (non exclusives) (%)', row Ensemble: Region TTA 7,5 8,2 7,8 / National 3,1 3,3 3,2 (Masculin, Feminin, Ensemble). National ensemble 3.2% confirmed. The census item is 'local languages used', not 'used in daily life'; wording aligned to the table.
results.text: Nationwide, 3.2% of Morocco's population reported Tarifit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

results.note: HCP Souss-Massa RGPH 2024 PDF: table 'Langues locales utilisees - Region de Souss-Massa' (Masculin Feminin Ensemble): 'Darija 82,1 76,3 79,2 / Tachelhit 62,9 63,5 63,2'. Ensemble 63.2% confirmed; evidence verbatim across a line break.

Same national table as irifiyen fact 1: row Ensemble 'Tachelhit 1,6 1,4 1,5 14,2 14,2 14,2'; National ensemble 14.2% confirmed. 'In daily life' is not the census wording; aligned to 'local languages used'.
results.text: Nationwide, 14.2% of Morocco's population reported Tachelhit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

Inalco page: 'Three varieties are currently taught at Inalco: Kabyle (taqbaylit, Algeria)...' and 'a complete Berber curriculum, from bachelor's degree to doctorate'. 'In Paris' not stated on page but correct.

IWGIA DRC chapter: term 'refers to the Mbuti, Baka and Batwa peoples ... They are widely acknowledged as the first inhabitants of the national rainforests'.

names.note: UNESCO page title uses 'Oromo'. Self-name in Afaan Oromoo is Oromoo; 'Oromo' is the standard published form.
UNESCO WHC page: 'Konso', 'Konso people'.
Cultural Survival page: 'the Anywaa (also spelled as Anuak)'.
pastoralists.org and IWGIA both use 'Afar'.
Cultural Survival uses 'Benet'; IWGIA uses 'Mosopisyek Benet people, also referred to as Ndorobo'. 'Mosopisyek' in also is correct.
Kara-Tunga page uses 'Karimojong'; IWGIA uses 'Karamojong' (in also).
Cultural Survival page uses both 'Hai//om' and 'Hai||om'; the Namibian uses 'Hai-//om'. The click letter form Haiǁom is in also.
IWGIA: 'the Tshwa (Tjwa, Cua) San'.
SAHO uses 'Korana' for the people, '!Orakua'/'!Orana' as self-reference, 'Kora' or '!Ora' for the language; IWGIA spells 'Koranna'.
SAHO article title 'Griqua'; IWGIA 'Griqua'.
Forest Peoples Programme uses 'Bagyeli'; IWGIA 'Bagyeli or Bakola'.
Cultural Survival page title 'wodaabe'; MSH Mondes 'wodaabe'; pastoralists.org 'Woodaabe' (in also).

Chapter uses 'Siwans' (heading 'Berbers, Siwans and Egyptians') and 'Siwi' for the language; the Siwi self-name Isiwan does not appear on this page, so it could not be verified here. If a source for 'Isiwan' is found, the contract would prefer it as the lead name.

name_source_url (HCP census PDF) never uses 'Irifiyen'; it only names the language Tarifit and 'Amazigh'. The endonym is plausible but unverified by the cited source; needs a name_source_url that shows 'Irifiyen' in use (e.g. a Rif cultural association or IRCAM page).

name_source_url (Inalco) does not contain 'Ishelhin' (checked: Ishelhin, Ichelhiyen, Ishelhiyen all absent); it uses 'Chleuh (tachelhit, southern Morocco)'. Name unverified by the cited source; needs a source showing the endonym.
name_source_url (Inalco) does not contain 'Iqbayliyen'; it uses 'Kabyle (taqbaylit, Algeria)'. Name unverified by the cited source; needs a source showing the endonym.
name_source_url (UNESCO M'Zab Valley) uses 'Mozabite' and 'M'Zab' only; 'At Mzab' does not appear. Name unverified by the cited source; needs a source showing 'At Mzab' / 'Ath Mzab' in use.

IWGIA Cameroon and Gabon chapters use 'Baka'.
IWGIA uses 'Khoikhoi' (also spelled Khoekhoe on the same page: 'Cape Khoekhoe').
UNEP story uses 'Samburu'.
UNESCO WHC and IWGIA use 'Mbuti'.
IWGIA uses 'Khwe' / 'Khwe San'.
IWGIA uses '!Xun'.
